title: Sensory Overload in Social Space
hook: The restaurant you chose for its buzz may be, for the person across the table, a wall of noise that leaves nothing over for conversation.
why:
Every social setting is also a sensory one: light, noise, smell, crowding, touch. For most people, most of the time, the senses sit in the background while attention goes to the conversation. For many people they do not. Autistic people, people with ADHD, people with hearing loss, migraine or chronic pain, and anyone exhausted or hungover can find that the room itself takes all their capacity, leaving little for the person in front of them.

When that happens, the body changes in ways that are easily misread: a flat face, short answers, a hand over one ear, eyes on the floor, a sudden need to leave. A reader who does not consider the room will read these as rudeness, boredom, coldness or drunkenness.

This chapter covers how differently people experience the same room, what overload looks like, why noise in particular eats conversation, the condition in which specific sounds provoke rage, how ordinary accommodation has become, how to respond to someone who is overloaded, and how to notice your own threshold. It applies to everyone, but it matters most for the people this part of the book is about.

teach.p:
In 2009 Laura Crane, Lorna Goddard and Linda Pring asked autistic and non-autistic adults to complete a questionnaire about how they responded to everyday sensations. More than nine in ten of the autistic adults scored at an extreme level on at least one dimension, compared with far fewer of the others. The researchers also found striking variation among the autistic adults themselves.

That variation matters. Some people are over-responsive: ordinary sounds are painfully loud, fluorescent lights flicker visibly, the label in a shirt is a constant irritation. Others are under-responsive and seek out strong sensations, such as deep pressure, loud music or constant movement. Many people are both, depending on the sense and the day. In 2017 Caroline Robertson and Simon Baron-Cohen reviewed the research and argued that sensory differences are among the most common and least understood features of autism.

Sensory differences are not limited to autism. People with ADHD often describe being unable to filter out background noise. People with hearing loss struggle in exactly the settings where others relax. Anyone who is ill, in pain, sleep-deprived or anxious has a lower threshold than usual.

For a reader, the lesson is to stop assuming that the room you are in is the room the other person is in. A pub you find lively may be, for someone else, a place where every sound arrives at once at full volume. The figure here covers his eyes with one hand. In a bright, loud room this may be the only way he can stay in it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic and non-autistic adults experienced everyday sensations in much the same way. Crane and colleagues found more than nine in ten autistic adults at an extreme level on at least one sensory dimension.

teach.p:
Sensory overload has a recognisable shape, though it varies from person to person. Early on, people often try to reduce the input: a hand to the ear, a squint, turning away from a light, retreating to the edge of a room, putting on headphones or sunglasses. Movement may increase, as people use stimming, rocking or fiddling to regulate themselves.

As overload builds, conversation suffers. Answers get shorter. The face goes flat. Eye contact, already difficult for some, disappears. People may become irritable, snap at small things, or say they need to leave without explanation.

At the extreme, autistic people describe two kinds of response. A shutdown looks like going quiet and unresponsive, sometimes unable to speak. A meltdown looks like a loss of control, with shouting, crying or distress that cannot be stopped by reasoning. Neither is a tantrum or a choice. Both are the nervous system reaching its limit.

Outside observers often misread all of this. Short answers are taken as rudeness, leaving early as unfriendliness, a flat face as boredom, a meltdown as bad behaviour or drunkenness. The first useful question, when someone seems to be withdrawing in a busy place, is whether the place is the problem. The figure here covers his mouth and looks down, a posture of holding something in.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if withdrawal in busy places usually reflected dislike of the company. Autistic people's accounts, and the sensory research, suggest that the setting itself is often the cause.

teach.p:
Of all the senses, hearing does most to shape social settings, because conversation depends on it. In a noisy room, people raise their voices to be heard. Everyone else then raises theirs, and the noise climbs. This is called the Lombard effect, after the French doctor who described it in 1911, and it explains why busy restaurants grow louder as the evening goes on.

For someone with typical hearing and no sensory differences, the cost is mild: a hoarse voice and some missed words. For someone with hearing loss, the cost is high, because background noise masks exactly the consonants they already struggle to hear. For many autistic people and people with ADHD, who find it harder to filter out competing sounds, a noisy room can make following a conversation nearly impossible, however hard they try.

The effort of listening in noise is tiring in itself, and tiredness shows in the body: slumping, glazed attention, nodding along without following. Someone who seems disengaged at a loud dinner may be working harder than anyone at the table just to keep up.

The choice of setting is therefore part of the message you send. Choosing a loud venue for an important conversation, or for meeting someone you know struggles with noise, says something even if you never meant it to. The figures here sit across a table, close enough to hear each other. In a quiet room, that is easy. In a loud one, it is work.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if background noise affected everyone's ability to follow conversation equally. People with hearing loss, and many neurodivergent people, are disproportionately affected.
teach.pullQuote: The choice of setting is part of the message you send.

teach.p:
Some people react intensely to particular sounds, most often sounds that other people make with their mouths or noses: chewing, slurping, breathing, sniffing, or repetitive sounds such as pen-clicking. The reaction is not mild annoyance. It is a surge of anger, disgust or panic, often with a strong urge to leave or to make the sound stop.

This is called misophonia. In 2022 Susan Swedo and a panel of experts agreed a consensus definition, describing it as a disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds or stimuli associated with them, which provoke strong negative emotional and physiological responses. It can occur on its own and alongside other conditions.

Misophonia is easy to misread from outside, because the person reacting may appear to be angry at you personally. They may glare, tense their jaw, put their hands over their ears or leave the table during a meal. The reaction is involuntary. Most people with misophonia know it is out of proportion, and many feel ashamed of it.

If someone tells you they have it, take it at face value. Small changes, such as eating apart, background music to mask the trigger, or simply not making the sound near them, cost little. If you are the one reacting, it helps to name it rather than leave others to guess: It's not you, certain sounds affect me badly. The figure here stands with arms crossed tightly, jaw set, a posture that may look like hostility and may be a struggle with a sound.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if strong reactions to chewing and breathing sounds were simply bad temper. The consensus definition describes an involuntary emotional and physiological response to specific sounds.

teach.p:
For a long time, people who found busy places overwhelming were expected to cope or stay away. That has begun to change, and the changes show how small adjustments can widen who is able to take part.

In July 2018 the British supermarket chain Morrisons, working with the National Autistic Society, introduced a weekly Quieter Hour across its stores. For one hour on Saturday mornings, lights were dimmed, music and radio were switched off, announcements were avoided and checkout noise was reduced. Other retailers, cinemas, museums and sports grounds have introduced similar quiet times, relaxed performances and sensory rooms.

The same logic applies to individuals. Noise-cancelling headphones, sunglasses indoors, a hat brim, fidget objects and sitting near a door are all ways people make a setting manageable. To an observer who does not know this, they can look rude or odd: a man in headphones at a family gathering, sunglasses in a meeting room. They are better read as tools that let the person stay.

If someone uses them, do not ask them to stop. If you are hosting, think about offering a quieter room, a seat away from the speakers, a dimmer light or a break outside. The figure here sits with headphones on and gaze lowered. Without them, he might not be in the room at all.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if reducing light and noise made no difference to who could take part. The spread of quiet hours and relaxed performances, developed with autistic people, reflects demand from people who could not otherwise attend.

teach.p:
When someone is overloaded, the instinct to help often makes things worse. Asking a stream of questions, touching their arm, crowding in to check they are all right or insisting they explain what is wrong all add input to a system that already has too much.

The better response is to subtract. Lower your voice and use fewer words. Offer one simple choice: Do you want to step outside? Avoid touch unless you know it is welcome. Give space, and reduce the light, noise or crowd if you can. Do not demand eye contact or an explanation.

If someone is in shutdown or meltdown, safety comes first. Make sure they are not in danger, keep others back, and wait. Reasoning rarely helps in the moment; calm presence does. Afterwards, do not make it a big deal. Many people feel embarrassed after a meltdown, and the kindest response is to treat it as ordinary.

The same principles help anyone who is overwhelmed, whether by noise, grief or panic. Part II's chapter on anxiety described a similar approach. The figures here sit side by side on a bench, quiet, neither looking at the other. Sometimes the most helpful thing is simply to be there without adding anything.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if asking questions and offering reassurance helped someone in sensory overload as much as reducing input. Autistic people's accounts consistently describe additional input as making overload worse.

teach.p:
It is easy to read this chapter as being about other people. But everyone has a sensory threshold, and it moves.

Part II described how sleep loss, illness, hunger and stress lower tolerance. A man who copes easily with a loud bar on a Friday night may find the same bar unbearable after a week of poor sleep. Hangovers make light and noise painful. Hearing changes with age, often without the person noticing, so that noisy rooms gradually become harder to follow. The later chapter on age looks at this.

Knowing your own threshold helps in two ways. It lets you notice when your irritability or withdrawal in a busy place comes from the setting rather than the people, so you do not take it out on them. And it gives you a small, direct sense of what many neurodivergent people live with all the time.

It also gives you permission to make adjustments for yourself: choosing quieter places for conversations that matter, taking breaks outside, wearing ear protection at concerts, leaving before you are overwhelmed rather than after. The figure here breathes out slowly, the long exhale that helps the nervous system settle when a room has been too much.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if sensory tolerance were fixed regardless of sleep, illness and stress. Part II reviewed evidence that these lower tolerance, which is why the same room can feel different on different days.

caseStudy:
Jamal, thirty-one, meets his old school friends every month at a sports bar near the station: big screens, loud music, standing room only. His friend Pete always comes, but lately he has been quiet, standing at the edge, answering in single words and leaving after an hour. The others joked that Pete had become boring since he got married.

One evening Jamal walked out with Pete to the station and asked if everything was all right. Pete hesitated, then said that he had been diagnosed with ADHD that year, and that the bar was, for him, like trying to listen to five radios at once. He could not follow what anyone was saying, and by the end of the night he had a headache and nothing left. He had not wanted to make a fuss.

Jamal suggested they try somewhere quieter. The group grumbled, but agreed to alternate: one month the sports bar, the next a pub with a back room where they could sit round a table. In the quieter pub, Pete was a different person: funny, quick and full of stories. Two of the others admitted they could hear better there too.

Jamal also noticed his own pattern. After a week of bad sleep, he found the sports bar much harder than usual, and had once snapped at a friend for no reason. He started telling the group when he was tired, and leaving earlier on those nights, without making a thing of it. Nobody seemed to mind, and the evenings were better for it.
observe: Notice the sensory setting of your next social event: the noise, light and crowding, and who seems most affected by it.
Notice anyone who withdraws, leaves early or uses headphones or sunglasses indoors, and consider whether the setting is the cause.
Notice your own threshold this week: when noise or light made you irritable, and what else was going on that day.
Notice how loud the places you choose for important conversations are, and whether you could hear the other person easily.

drills.name: Room Audit
steps: Before your next social event, picture the room: noise, music, light, crowding, smells.
Rate it from one to five for how easy it would be to hold a quiet conversation.
If it rates low, find one adjustment: a quieter corner, a table away from speakers, a walk outside.
Afterwards, note whether the adjustment changed how anyone behaved.
variations: Audit a place you go every week, such as a café or a gym, and rate it at two different times of day.
Ask someone who finds busy places hard to rate a venue with you, and compare their rating with yours.
Add light and smell to your audit, not just sound, and notice which of the three bothers you most.

drills.name: Subtract, Don't Add
steps: Think of someone you know who gets overwhelmed in busy places.
Write down what you usually do when they seem to be struggling.
Cross out anything that adds input: questions, touch, reassurance at length.
Replace it with one subtracting response, such as a single quiet offer to step outside.
variations: Practise your one quiet offer aloud, so that it comes out calmly when you need it.
Next time someone is upset in a busy place, try saying half as much as you normally would, and notice what happens.
Ask someone you know who gets overwhelmed what they would most like people to do, and what they would most like people to stop doing.

drills.name: Threshold Diary
steps: For one week, note each time noise, light or crowding bothered you.
Record how you slept the night before and how stressed you were.
Look for a pattern between your state and your tolerance.
Choose one adjustment for days when your threshold is low.
variations: Note your caffeine and alcohol alongside sleep and stress, and see whether they change your tolerance for noise.
On a low-threshold day, try one small adjustment, such as earplugs on the train, and note whether it changes your mood later.
Notice whether your irritability with the people at home tends to follow noisy, crowded days at work.

drills.name: Choose the Quiet Venue
steps: For your next important one-to-one conversation, choose the setting deliberately.
Pick somewhere you could hear a person speaking at normal volume from across a small table.
Notice how the conversation compares with ones held in louder places.
Keep a short list of quiet places you can suggest.
variations: Suggest a walk instead of a café for your next catch-up, and compare the conversation with your usual ones.
Ask a colleague who wears hearing aids which meeting rooms they find easiest, and book those for meetings they attend.
Find two quiet places near your work or home where you could take someone for an important conversation, and note them down.

quiz.q: A relative wears noise-cancelling headphones throughout a family gathering. Someone says it is rude and antisocial. What does this chapter suggest?
options: It is rude, because headphones always signal that someone wants to shut others out
Headphones may be how he manages the noise well enough to stay at the gathering
It shows he is listening to music and has no interest in the family conversation
It means he is autistic, so the family should treat him differently from now on
quiz.explain: Headphones, sunglasses indoors and similar tools are often ways of making a setting bearable. Asking someone to remove them may mean they leave altogether.

quiz.q: What did Crane, Goddard and Pring find about sensory processing in autistic adults?
options: More than nine in ten scored at an extreme level on at least one sensory dimension
Autistic adults all responded to sensations in exactly the same over-sensitive way
Sensory differences disappeared in adulthood, once people had learned how to cope
Autistic adults were less sensitive than others on every sensory dimension tested
quiz.explain: More than nine in ten autistic adults scored at an extreme level on at least one dimension, and there was striking variation among them, with some over- and some under-responsive. The same room can be a very different place for each of them.

quiz.q: How does the 2022 consensus definition describe misophonia?
options: A preference for quiet, which people choose and can change if they want
A form of hearing loss that makes everyday sounds seem much louder
Decreased tolerance to specific sounds, provoking strong negative responses
Bad manners, shown by people who dislike how others eat or breathe
quiz.explain: Misophonia involves decreased tolerance of specific sounds, such as chewing or breathing, which provoke strong emotional and physiological reactions. The reaction is involuntary.

quiz.q: Which changes did Morrisons' Quieter Hour, developed with the National Autistic Society, include?
options: Extra staff on the doors, to hand out leaflets about autism to every customer
Louder announcements, so that customers could hear clearly over the background
Longer opening hours, so that customers could shop at any time of the night
Dimmed lights, music switched off and quieter checkouts for one hour a week
quiz.explain: For one hour on Saturday mornings, lights were dimmed, music and radio were switched off, announcements were avoided and checkout noise was reduced. Small changes like these widen who is able to come at all.

quiz.q: At a crowded party, a friend has gone quiet, has one hand over his ear and is looking at the floor. What fits this chapter best?
options: Lower your voice, offer one quiet option to step outside, and avoid touching him
Put an arm round him and ask him several questions to find out what is wrong
Leave him alone completely, since he clearly does not want anyone near him
Ask him loudly whether he has had too much to drink, so that others can help
quiz.explain: When someone is overloaded, subtract input: fewer words, a single simple choice, space and no unexpected touch. Questions and reassurance add to the load.

quiz.q: A colleague has mentioned that loud places make it hard for him to follow conversations. You need to discuss a project with him. Where should you meet?
options: At the busy café downstairs, since it is the most convenient for both of you
A quiet meeting room, or a walk outside, where normal voices can be heard
At the after-work drinks, so that the meeting feels more relaxed and social
Over a video call with the office noise in the background, to save time
quiz.explain: Choosing a quiet setting makes the conversation possible for him and is itself a signal that you listened. Noise affects people with hearing or sensory differences far more than others.

quiz.q: What is the Lombard effect, described by a French doctor in 1911?
options: The way people speak more slowly in quiet rooms, so that conversations take longer
The way people raise their voices in noise, so that a noisy room grows steadily louder
The way light from screens makes people more alert and talkative in the evening
The way people stop talking altogether once the background noise passes a certain set level
quiz.explain: In noise, people raise their voices to be heard, everyone else then raises theirs, and the noise climbs. It is why busy restaurants get louder as the evening goes on.

quiz.q: In a crowded supermarket, a seven-year-old has a meltdown, screaming and hitting his head, while his father kneels beside him. What fits this chapter best?
options: Tell the father firmly that the boy needs discipline, so that he learns how to behave
Offer one quiet choice, such as a dim room nearby, and otherwise give them space
Ask the boy a series of questions to find out exactly what has upset him so much
Lift the boy up and carry him outside quickly, whatever he and his father want
quiz.explain: A meltdown is a loss of control that reasoning cannot stop, not a tantrum. Subtracting input, keeping him safe and offering one quiet option helps far more than questions, touch or comments.

quiz.q: Someone says sensory overload in social settings only happens to autistic people. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That many people can be overwhelmed, including people with hearing loss, and thresholds move
That only autistic children are affected, and that adults grow out of it with time and practice
That overload is always a choice, and anyone can push through a loud room if they want to
That only people with misophonia experience overload, since it is a single condition
quiz.explain: Hearing loss, ADHD, migraine, tiredness, illness and stress can all lower someone's tolerance for noise and light, and everyone's threshold moves from day to day. Choosing calmer settings helps all of them.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific social occasion in the past few months when you, or someone with you, struggled with the setting: the noise, the light, the crowd. Describe the room and what the struggle looked like in the body: withdrawal, irritability, leaving early, covering ears or eyes. How was it read by others at the time? Having read this chapter, what would you change about the setting, or about how you responded, if the same occasion came round again?
reflection.guidance: The aim is to notice the room as part of every reading. Be specific about the sensory details and about the behaviour that followed. If it was you who struggled, consider what else was affecting your threshold that day, such as sleep or stress.

failureMode: The first failure is to assume that the room you are in is the room everyone is in, when sensory experience varies enormously between people. The second is to read withdrawal, short answers or leaving early in a busy place as rudeness, when the setting may be the cause. The third is to choose loud venues for conversations that matter. The fourth is to read an involuntary reaction to a sound as personal anger. The fifth is to ask someone to remove headphones or sunglasses that let them stay. The sixth is to respond to overload by adding input, with questions, touch and reassurance. And the seventh is to ignore your own threshold, and blame others for irritability that comes from the room.

moreCases.title: The grandfather outside the marquee
moreCases.scene:
Frank, sixty-eight, has been looking forward to his granddaughter Chloe's wedding for a year. The ceremony goes beautifully. The reception is in a marquee in a field, with a ten-piece band, a wooden dance floor and two hundred guests. By the time the speeches are over and the band starts, the marquee is very loud.

Frank has had some hearing loss for several years. He has hearing aids, which he wears in quiet rooms and leaves in his pocket in noisy ones, because they turn everything into the same roar. Within half an hour of the band starting, he cannot follow anything anyone says to him. He nods, smiles, guesses and gets things wrong. Someone asks him whether he is enjoying himself and he answers a different question. After an hour he goes outside and sits on a hay bale by the car park, alone, with his tie loosened.

Inside, the family notices. His son-in-law says Frank has never warmed to the groom. An aunt says he always did sulk at parties. Chloe, who has seen him go out, is hurt, and wonders whether he disapproves of something.

Her new husband, Sam, goes out to find him and sits down on the next hay bale. Frank says, in the relative quiet, that it has been the best day of his life and that he cannot hear a single word in there.

He had tried putting the hearing aids in during the speeches, which had worked, and then the band had started and the first chord had made him wince so badly that he took them straight out again.

Frank's wife, Jean, who died four years ago, used to do the talking for both of them at loud parties, standing at his elbow and repeating what people said. Without her, he has quietly stopped going to most of them.

His grandson, Ben, eleven, had tried to talk to him about football twice, and Frank had answered both times with "Lovely," which Ben had found funny and then slightly worrying.
moreCases.misread:
The family read Frank's withdrawal, his wrong answers and his retreat outside as sulking or disapproval of the marriage. Frank had read his own struggle as something to hide, and had chosen to sit alone rather than explain.

Frank had also misread himself, in a way: he had decided that a man who could not hear at his granddaughter's wedding had no business being in the middle of it, and taken himself away.

Chloe's hurt was a reading too, built on a quick glimpse of her grandfather walking out during the first dance. From inside a crowded marquee, it looked like a man who had had enough of her wedding.

Frank's son-in-law had in fact once had a disagreement with Frank about politics, years ago, and the memory made his reading feel like evidence.
moreCases.betterRead:
Background noise masks exactly the consonants that people with hearing loss already struggle to hear, as this chapter describes, and in a marquee with a band, the Lombard effect pushes every voice louder until the whole room is a wall of sound. Frank's nods, guesses and retreat were the ordinary results of a setting that had taken away his ability to follow conversation. Nothing in them was about the groom. Sam's better response subtracted rather than added: he sat beside Frank in the quiet and listened. Then he and Chloe set up two chairs outside the marquee, by a lamp, and took turns bringing family members out to sit with Frank for ten minutes at a time. Frank had a proper conversation with nearly everyone he loved, one at a time, in the quiet. Chloe said later that the hay bales were her favourite part of the evening.

Frank wore his hearing aids for the quiet conversations outside, and heard every word.

At the next family party, Chloe made sure there was a quiet corner, and Frank stayed until the end.

moreCases.title: The crisps on the sofa
moreCases.scene:
Leo, twenty-six, and his partner, Hana, twenty-five, have just moved in together. On their third evening in the new flat, they settle down to watch a film. Hana opens a bag of crisps. Within a minute, Leo's jaw has tightened, his shoulders have gone up and he is staring at the screen with a fixed expression. When Hana crunches again, he says sharply, "Can you not?", gets up and goes to the kitchen.

Hana is stunned. Leo is usually gentle and easy-going. She sits on the sofa wondering what she has done, whether he is angry with her about something else, and whether moving in together was a mistake. When he comes back, she asks what is wrong. He says, "Nothing," and sits at the other end of the sofa.

It happens again two days later, at breakfast, when she eats an apple. This time Leo puts in his earbuds and turns away from the table. Hana feels rejected and says so. Leo apologises, says it is not about her, and then cannot explain what it is about.

A week later, Hana finds an article about misophonia on her phone, and recognises everything in it. She shows it to Leo. He reads it twice. Then he tells her that he has felt this way about chewing sounds since he was about eleven, and that he has never told anyone, because it sounded mad.

Hana had also noticed, over the months they had been dating, that Leo always chose noisy restaurants and never wanted to eat at her parents' quiet kitchen table. She had thought he simply liked a buzz.

Leo's mother, when he tells her, says that he used to leave the table at Sunday lunch as a boy and that they had put it down to him being difficult. She is upset that she never asked.

Hana also remembers that Leo once walked out of a cinema halfway through a film when the man beside him opened a packet of sweets. At the time, he had said he felt ill.
moreCases.misread:
Hana read Leo's tension, sharp words and retreat as anger at her, and perhaps as a sign of deeper problems in the relationship. Leo read his own reaction as something shameful and irrational, and could not explain it even to himself.

And Leo's "nothing" was read as a closed door, when it was a man who had no words for what was happening to him.

She also read his earbuds at breakfast as a deliberate shutting out of her, the second rejection in a week, when they were the only way he could stay at the table at all.
moreCases.betterRead:
Swedo and colleagues' consensus definition describes misophonia as a decreased tolerance of specific sounds, which provoke strong negative emotional and physiological responses. The reaction is involuntary and can look exactly like personal anger, with a glare, a tight jaw and a sudden exit. Leo was not angry with Hana; his body was reacting to a sound before he could think. The better reading let both of them stop blaming. Together they agreed a few practical changes: background music or the television on during meals, crunchy snacks eaten in the kitchen when Leo was in the living room, earbuds when he needed them, without either of them taking it personally. Leo also saw his GP, who talked through options for support. Hana said that knowing what it was made it easier to stop feeling rejected, and Leo said that being believed was the biggest relief.

They also agreed a signal, a tap on the table, that Leo could use when a sound was getting to him, so that neither of them had to explain in the moment.

Within a few months, Hana barely noticed the arrangements, and Leo said the flat had become the easiest place he had ever lived.

moreCases.title: The headphones in the open-plan office
moreCases.scene:
Shreya, thirty-five, is a data scientist at an insurance company, and she is autistic. The company has just moved to a new open-plan office with glass walls, bright overhead lights, a coffee machine that hisses every few minutes and hot desks. By two in the afternoon on most days, Shreya has a headache, finds it hard to concentrate and has stopped speaking to anyone. She has started wearing noise-cancelling headphones from the moment she arrives, and sunglasses when the sun comes through the glass.

Her colleagues notice. One jokes in the team chat that Shreya is "in her bubble again". Another says, more seriously, to their manager, Paul, that she seems unfriendly and does not want to be part of the team. Paul, who is new, asks Shreya in a one-to-one whether she could take the headphones off more often, so that people feel they can approach her.

Shreya goes home and cries. The headphones are what let her get through the day. She considers resigning.

The next morning she emails Paul, carefully, to explain that she is autistic, that the office is overwhelming for her, and that the headphones and sunglasses are how she manages it. She asks whether there is a quieter space she could use.

She had mentioned to the facilities team, during the move, that she was worried about the lighting. She had been told that the new office was designed for wellbeing.

In meetings, she has started taking the headphones off and putting them round her neck, and finds that she can follow the conversation for about twenty minutes before the noise from the open office outside makes it impossible.

Paul, reading the email at his desk, realises that he had never once asked her why she wore them.

Shreya has also noticed that she says less in the afternoon stand-ups than in the morning ones, and that her manager has started directing his questions to her colleagues instead.
moreCases.misread:
Her colleagues read Shreya's headphones, sunglasses and silence as unfriendliness and a lack of interest in the team. Paul read them as a barrier to be removed, and asked her to remove the thing that was making the office bearable.

Paul also read the team's complaint as a fair concern about team spirit, without asking what the headphones were for.

The colleague who made the joke read the headphones as a choice about people, when they were a choice about noise. The team never asked which it was.

Shreya had also read Paul's request as a sign that her job was at risk, which is how many people hear a manager asking them to change something they cannot.
moreCases.betterRead:
Crane, Goddard and Pring found that the great majority of the autistic adults they studied reported extreme responses on at least one sensory dimension, and Robertson and Baron-Cohen described sensory differences as among the most common features of autism. An open-plan office with bright lights and constant noise can be, for some people, an exhausting place to be. Shreya's headphones were an adjustment, as ordinary as a pair of glasses. Paul's better response, after her email, was to apologise and to act. He found her a desk in a quieter corner away from the coffee machine, arranged a dimmer bank of lights above it, made it clear to the team that headphones were welcome for anyone, and asked colleagues to message Shreya rather than tap her on the shoulder. The joke in the chat stopped. Two other colleagues started using the quiet corner too.

Shreya stayed, and was promoted the following year.

Paul also changed the hot-desk rules so that anyone who needed a particular desk for health reasons could book it permanently.

She also asked the facilities team to add a quiet room to the next floor plan, and they did, after three other people asked for the same.

moreCases.title: The meltdown in the supermarket
moreCases.scene:
Darren, forty, takes his son Alfie, seven, who is autistic, to the supermarket on a Saturday afternoon, because Alfie's mother is working and they need food for the week. Darren knows the timing is bad, but there is no other option. The store is crowded, the lights are bright, a radio is playing, the tannoy keeps announcing offers, and a child in the next aisle is screaming.

Near the checkouts, Alfie stops walking, puts his hands over his ears and begins to rock. When Darren crouches down and asks him what is wrong, Alfie screams, throws himself to the floor and begins hitting his head with his hands. Darren tries to talk to him calmly, then to lift him; Alfie fights him off. A queue of people watches.

A woman behind them says, loudly, that what the boy needs is a firm hand. Another shopper films on her phone. Darren feels his face burning and his own heart pounding. He kneels on the floor, puts his body between Alfie and the trolley, and says nothing at all.

A young shop worker, Kemi, comes over. She does not ask questions. She says quietly to Darren that there is a staff room behind the bakery that is quiet and dim, and asks whether that would help.

Darren had tried to prepare Alfie in the car, explaining that it would be busy and that they would be quick. Alfie had nodded and asked whether there would be music. Darren had said he did not know.

Darren has been in this position before, in a play park and once at a family wedding. He knows it will pass. He also knows that the next ten minutes will feel like an hour.

An older man in the queue, Darren notices, has quietly moved his trolley to block the line of sight of the woman filming.
moreCases.misread:
The woman in the queue read Alfie's meltdown as a tantrum and his father's calm as weakness. The shopper filming read it as a spectacle. Both readings added pressure to a child whose nervous system had already gone past its limit.

Darren, too, felt the pull of their reading, and for a moment wondered whether he was handling it wrong. He held his ground, which was the right call.

The shopper filming also read the scene as public property, when it was a child in distress and a father doing his best.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes a meltdown as a loss of control that cannot be stopped by reasoning, not a tantrum or a choice, and the response that helps is to subtract input and keep the person safe. Darren's silence and his body between Alfie and the trolley were exactly right. Kemi's offer was the best kind of help: one quiet choice, no questions, a way to remove the noise and light. In the staff room, with the lights off, Alfie calmed within ten minutes. Kemi brought him a cup of water and left them alone. Afterwards Darren found out that the store held a weekly quieter hour, like the one Morrisons introduced with the National Autistic Society, with dimmed lights and no music or announcements. He shops then now. Kemi's manager put a note in the staff newsletter about what she had done, and the store trained its staff to offer the same.

Darren also wrote to the store manager to thank Kemi by name, which, she told him later, was the first letter of thanks she had ever received at work.

workedReading.title: Planning a team party everyone can enjoy
workedReading.scene:
Ruth, forty-seven, is office manager for a firm of accountants, and she has been asked to organise the end-of-year party for sixty people. The last two parties were at a bar in town with a DJ, and Ruth noticed both times that a handful of people left within an hour, that the older partners stood in the corridor to talk, and that one colleague who uses hearing aids did not come at all this year. She also knows that at least two members of staff are autistic and one has told her that loud venues are very hard for her. Ruth wants a party that the people who love dancing will still enjoy, and that does not quietly exclude everyone else. She decides to plan it with the senses in mind, using the Room Audit drill from this chapter, and to ask rather than guess what would help.

She also remembers that the colleague with hearing aids, when asked why he had missed the party, had said only that he did not really do parties any more, and that she had not asked further. She wishes now that she had.

She also knows that several of the firm's oldest clients are coming, and that some of them, in their seventies, have told her before that they cannot hear anything at loud events.

steps.label: Audit the venue
steps.text:
She visits three possible venues in person, at the time of day the party will be held. At each one she stands in the middle and tries to hold a quiet conversation with the events manager across a small table. The bar where they have always gone fails; she cannot hear a word. A hotel function room passes, with carpet, curtains and a separate lounge off the main room. She books the hotel.

She also checks where the toilets and the exits are, and whether the route to them goes through the loudest part of the room, since that decides whether people can step out easily.

She also asks each venue what else will be happening that night, and rules out one that has a wedding disco in the next room.

steps.label: Build in a quiet room
steps.text:
She asks the hotel to keep the lounge next to the function room as a quiet space all evening, with low lighting, comfortable chairs, no music and some food and drink. She plans to tell everyone about it on the invitation as an ordinary feature of the party, not as a special room for particular people, so that anyone can use it without having to explain why.

She also puts the quiet room on the floor plan she sends round, next to the bar and the cloakroom, so that it reads as just another part of the venue.

She also puts a couple of jigsaw puzzles and some board games in the lounge, so that it reads as a place to do something, not just a place to escape.

steps.label: Set the light and sound
steps.text:
She asks the band to keep the volume moderate for the first two hours, during dinner, and to save the loud set for later, when the dancing starts. She asks the hotel to avoid flashing lights and to keep a few wall lamps on rather than using only coloured spots. The Lombard effect means that a room which starts loud only gets louder, so starting quieter matters.

She also asks for the speeches to be given with a microphone at a moderate volume, near the quieter end of the room, so that people with hearing loss can follow them.

She also asks for the dinner tables to be round rather than long, so that people can hear the whole table without shouting down its length.

She also asks for the dessert to be served before the loud set, so that people who leave after dinner do not miss it.

steps.label: Ask, and make answering easy
steps.text:
Two weeks before the party, she sends a short message with the invitation: "If there's anything that would make the evening easier for you, such as where you'd like to sit, let me know, no explanation needed." Four people reply. One asks to sit near the door; one asks for a table away from the speakers; the colleague with hearing aids asks for a table in the quieter lounge for dinner.

She also makes sure that the replies come only to her, and that the seating requests are arranged quietly, without anyone being pointed out on the night.

She also notices that two of the four requests come from people she would never have guessed would find parties difficult, which reminds her why asking matters.

She also says, when one person apologises for being difficult, that it is not difficult at all, which is true.

steps.label: Watch for overload, gently
steps.text:
On the night, Ruth keeps half an eye on the room. When she sees one young analyst standing at the edge with a hand pressed to one ear, looking at the floor, she does not go over and ask a string of questions. She catches his eye, smiles and nods towards the lounge door. He nods back and goes through. Subtracting input, not adding it, is the help this chapter recommends.

Later, she sees him back in the main room, chatting at the edge of the dance floor. A short break had been enough.

She also checks on the colleague with hearing aids once, briefly, and he gives her a thumbs up from a table in the lounge, deep in conversation with a client.

She resists checking on him again. A second visit would have turned a quiet break into a fuss.

steps.label: Make leaving easy
steps.text:
At the end of dinner, before the loud set, the managing partner thanks everyone and says, lightly, that the band is about to get going, that the lounge will stay quiet all night, and that anyone who needs to head home should feel free. It gives everyone a clear, warm exit, and nobody has to slip away feeling rude.

She also arranges taxis to be ordered from the hotel lobby, which is quiet, so that nobody has to stand outside the main room on the phone trying to hear a dispatcher.

She also arranges for the coats to be in the lounge, so that leaving does not mean pushing through the dance floor.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Almost everyone stays for dinner, more than at any party in years. The dancers dance. The lounge is busy all night, with partners, parents, the colleague with hearing aids and several people Ruth had not expected. One of the autistic colleagues tells her it is the first work party she has enjoyed. Ruth keeps her notes for next year: hear across a table, quiet room for all, quieter first half, ask, nod, easy exits.

The colleague with hearing aids sends her an email the next day saying it was the first party in years he had been able to follow, and asking whether the firm could use the same hotel for the summer lunch.

She also asks a few people, the following week, what would have made it even better. Two say the same thing: a slightly earlier end to the loud set.

moreFailures.title: Joking about someone's adjustment
moreFailures.body:
Headphones at a party, sunglasses indoors, earplugs at a concert, a hood up in a supermarket, a seat by the door: each is a way someone makes a setting bearable, and each is an easy target for a joke. "In your bubble again?", "Expecting the paparazzi?", "Are we that boring?" The jokes are usually meant lightly. To the person on the receiving end, they say that the thing which lets them stay is something to be embarrassed about, and they can push people towards taking the adjustment off, putting up with the pain, or not coming at all. Shreya nearly resigned over a chat message about her bubble. If you notice an adjustment, the kindest response is no response: do not comment, do not stare, and treat it as ordinary. If you are curious, and you know the person well, you can ask privately whether there is anything that would help.

If someone else makes the joke, a simple change of subject is often enough to stop it spreading.

And if you are the one with the adjustment, it is fine to say, lightly, "It helps me concentrate," and leave it there.

The person who chooses an adjustment has usually thought about it far more than the person tempted to joke about it.

moreFailures.title: Treating sensory needs as fussiness
moreFailures.body:
Some people respond to sensory difficulties with impatience: "You'll get used to it," "Everyone finds it loud," "Just ignore it." The assumption is that the discomfort is a matter of attitude, and that pushing through will make it go away. For many people with sensory differences, it does not work like that. Crane, Goddard and Pring found extreme sensory responses to be very common among autistic adults, and Robertson and Baron-Cohen described sensory differences as a core feature of autism, not a preference. Pushing through can lead to exhaustion, shutdown or meltdown rather than adaptation. The same is true of misophonia, which is involuntary. Treat a sensory need as you would treat any other practical need, such as a need to sit down or to see the screen clearly: something to accommodate, not something to argue with.

A useful test is to ask whether you would tell someone who needed glasses to just try harder to see.

It can also help to remember that what looks like a small noise to you may be, to someone else, like a fire alarm.

Accommodation costs the person who needs it nothing, and it usually costs everyone else very little.

moreFailures.title: Assuming overload belongs to autistic people only
moreFailures.body:
This chapter draws heavily on research about autism, but autistic people are far from the only ones for whom busy places can become too much. People with hearing loss struggle to follow speech in noise, as Frank did. People with ADHD can find competing sounds very hard to filter. People who get migraines may be sensitive to light and noise. People with tinnitus, people recovering from a head injury, people living with chronic pain or fatigue, people with a history of trauma, and anyone who has slept badly or is unwell may all have lower thresholds on some days. The safest assumption is that, in any group, some people are finding the room harder than you are. Choose settings that leave room for them, without needing to know who they are or why.

Choosing settings that work for the person with the lowest threshold tends to make them better for everyone else too.

It is also worth noticing your own threshold on your worst days, which gives you a small glimpse of how others may feel on most days.

In practice, this means defaulting to the quieter venue, the softer lighting and the earlier start, and letting people opt into the loud parts.

moreFailures.title: Making a big deal of it afterwards
moreFailures.body:
After a shutdown or meltdown, or after someone has had to leave a room suddenly, many people feel embarrassed, exhausted or ashamed. Well-meaning friends and colleagues can make this worse: asking in front of others whether they are all right now, asking them to explain what happened, telling the group about it, or treating them as fragile for weeks. The chapter's advice is to treat it as ordinary. A brief, private "Glad you're OK, let me know if there's anything that would help next time" is usually enough. Do not demand an explanation or a post-mortem. If the person wants to talk about it, they will, and it helps if you listen without alarm. What they will remember is not the meltdown but whether the people around them made them feel safe or watched.

If the meltdown happened at work, agree with the person what, if anything, will be said to colleagues, and say no more than that.

And if you were the one who had to leave, you do not owe anyone an account of why.

questions.q: How can I tell whether someone is overloaded or just not enjoying themselves?
questions.a:
Often you cannot tell from outside, and you do not need to. The early signs of overload described in this chapter, such as a hand to the ear, squinting, retreating to the edge of the room, shorter answers, a flat face or increased fidgeting, can also mean tiredness, boredom or worry. The useful response is the same either way: offer a quieter option, simply, without questions. "It's loud in here, want to step outside for a bit?" gives someone a way out if they need it and costs nothing if they do not. Avoid asking them to explain, and avoid assuming they are not enjoying your company. Frank's family assumed he disapproved of the groom; what he needed was a chair outside the marquee.

And if they say they are fine, believe them, and leave the offer open: "If you change your mind, I'll come with you."

It can also help to notice who chose the venue. If it was you, the quiet offer is part of being a good host.

questions.q: What should I do if someone has a meltdown or shutdown?
questions.a:
Make sure they are safe, then subtract. Move anything they could hurt themselves on, keep other people back and, if you can, reduce the noise and light, or offer a quieter place, as Kemi did. Use very few words, in a low voice, or none at all. Do not touch them unless you know it is welcome, and do not try to reason with them in the moment, which rarely helps. Wait. Calm presence matters more than anything you can say. If you are a bystander, the most helpful things are often not to stare, not to film, not to comment and to offer practical help to the person with them. Afterwards, treat it as ordinary, and do not ask for an explanation. If anyone is at risk of serious harm, get help.

It can also help, if you are with someone who has meltdowns, to agree a plan in advance, while things are calm.

It also helps, if you know someone is prone to meltdowns, to learn their early signs from them, so that you can help them leave sooner.

And if it is your own child, be kind to yourself afterwards. Staying calm in front of a staring queue is hard.

questions.q: How can I choose a venue that works for most people?
questions.a:
Use the test in this chapter: can you hear someone speaking at normal volume from across a small table? Visit at the time of day you will use it, because a quiet café at ten can be loud at one. Soft furnishings, carpet and curtains absorb sound; tiles, glass and high ceilings amplify it. Back rooms, booths and corners away from speakers and kitchens are usually quieter. Daytime and early evening are often calmer than late at night. For larger events, build in a quiet room open to everyone, keep music moderate at first and avoid flashing lights. For important one-to-one conversations, choose the quiet option every time. People will often tell you they would have been fine anywhere, and the conversation will be better regardless.

If you are not sure, ask the people you are meeting where they find easy, which also tells them you care about their comfort.

It is worth keeping a short list of such places in your phone, so that you can suggest one quickly when someone asks.

And if you are the guest, it is fine to suggest a quieter place. Most people will be glad you did.

questions.q: What is misophonia, and how can I live with someone who has it?
questions.a:
Swedo and colleagues' consensus definition describes misophonia as a decreased tolerance of specific sounds, often sounds made by other people's mouths or noses, such as chewing or breathing, which provoke strong negative emotional and physiological reactions. The reactions are involuntary and can look like anger at the person making the sound. Living with it is easier when both people understand that it is not personal. Agree practical arrangements together, such as background sound at meals, eating certain foods elsewhere and earbuds when needed, as Leo and Hana did, and treat them as ordinary. If the reactions are severe or affecting daily life, talk to a GP about support. Avoid teasing or deliberately making the sounds, which can make the reactions worse and damage trust.

It can also help to talk about it when you are both calm, not in the middle of a reaction, when neither of you can think clearly.

It also helps to remember that the person with misophonia often feels ashamed of the reaction, so kindness about it goes a long way.

questions.q: Why do noisy places seem to get harder as I get older?
questions.a:
Often because hearing changes with age, gradually and usually without the person noticing. The first thing to go is often the ability to pick out speech from background noise, especially the high-pitched consonants that distinguish one word from another. So a busy restaurant that was once merely lively becomes a place where you nod and guess. Tiredness, poor sleep and stress also lower tolerance at any age. If you find yourself struggling to follow conversations in noise, asking people to repeat themselves often, or avoiding social events you used to enjoy, it is worth having your hearing tested. Hearing aids, choosing quieter venues and sitting with your back to the noise all help. The later chapter on age in this part looks at how hearing loss can be misread as withdrawal.

It is also worth telling friends and family, so that they can choose quieter places and face you when they speak.

Facing the person you are talking to, in good light, also helps, because you will lip-read more than you realise.

questions.q: How can I make a workplace easier on the senses?
questions.a:
Start by asking people what they find hard, and make it easy to answer without explaining why. Common changes include quiet zones or rooms, desks away from kitchens and doors, dimmable or natural lighting rather than harsh overhead tubes, permission to wear headphones or sunglasses without comment, warning before fire alarm tests, and the option to message rather than tap someone on the shoulder, as Paul arranged for Shreya. In meetings, a quieter room and one person speaking at a time help everyone, especially people with hearing loss or sensory differences. In many countries, employers must consider reasonable adjustments for disabled staff, which can include sensory ones. Most of these changes cost little and benefit far more people than the ones who asked.

It also helps to ask people again after a few months, because needs change and new staff arrive with needs of their own.

It can also help to run a short, anonymous survey after any office move, asking specifically about noise and light.

And it helps to remember that the people who complain least are often the ones who have given up asking.

watch.title: Can you make it to the end?
watch.notice: A short film from inside a shopping centre as an autistic boy experiences it. Notice how ordinary sounds and lights pile up, and how his withdrawal would look from outside to someone who could not hear what he hears.

watch.title: Make it Stop
watch.notice: Another short film of overload from the inside. Notice the moment the body starts to protect itself, and what the people around could have done to subtract rather than add.

watch.title: Misophonia and the science of horrible sounds
watch.notice: Researchers and people with misophonia describe the reaction to sounds like chewing. Notice how strongly involuntary the response is, and how easily it could be mistaken for personal anger.

reviewPrompt: This week, choose a quiet place for one important conversation, and when someone seems overwhelmed, subtract rather than add.
